## Why are we here?

::: {.statement}
Modern science is increasingly **computational science**.
:::

## Reproducibility is hard

::: {.prompt}
Why can researchers fail to reproduce results when re-analyzing existing data?
:::

::: {.prompt}
What can we do to make our analyses easier to reproduce?
:::

::: {.aside}
Discuss in small groups for 3–4 minutes.
:::

## A common problem

::: {.quote-box}
Point-and-click analysis leaves very little record of **what was done, in what order, and with which settings**.
:::

Repeated manual steps are often:

- tedious
- difficult to audit
- difficult to share
- easy to do slightly differently the next time

## Reproducible workflows create a paper trail

:::: {.card-row}

::: {.panel}
**Code**

Records the analytical steps
:::

::: {.panel}
**Version control**

Records how files change over time
:::

::: {.panel}
**Reproducible documents**

Connect code, results, figures, and narrative
:::

::::

## The payoff

::: {.hero}
Better science  
**in less time**  
and with less pain
:::

## Who benefits?

:::: {.card-row}

::: {.panel}
**Future you**

Less re-learning, fewer mysteries, faster progress
:::

::: {.panel}
**Collaborators**

Clearer workflows and easier handoffs
:::

::: {.panel}
**Science**

More transparency and more opportunities to catch errors
:::

- Your name

## What do we mean by “data science”?

::: {.statement}
Turning raw data into **understanding, insight, and knowledge**
:::

## A major theme of this course

::: {.quote-box}
Do not build your analysis around whatever strange format your data happened to arrive in.
:::

Instead, deliberately create structures that make analysis:

- easier to reason about
- easier to reuse
- easier to communicate
- easier to reproduce

## By the end of the course, you should be able to…

- build reproducible, project-oriented workflows in RStudio
- import, clean, reorganize, and combine messy data
- explore and visualize data effectively with **ggplot2**
- write simple functions and automate repeated tasks
- use **Git and GitHub** for version control and collaboration
- use **Quarto** to combine narrative, code, figures, and results
- use **AI as a coding partner while critically evaluating its output**

## What this course is *not*

:::: {.card-row .two}

::: {.panel}
**We will not focus on**

- statistical inference
- modeling and simulation
- very large-scale computing
- domain-specific analysis pipelines
:::




::::

## Why R?

- Free and open source
- Available across platforms
- Huge ecosystem for data manipulation, statistics, visualization, and communication
- Strong research community
- Excellent support for reproducible reports and workflows

::: {.accent-box}
We will focus mainly on the **tidyverse** approach to working with data.
:::

## The tidyverse

::: {.statement}
A coherent collection of R packages designed for data science
:::

`ggplot2` · `dplyr` · `tidyr` · `readr` · `purrr` · `tibble` · `stringr` · `forcats`

## How lectures and labs differ

:::: {.card-row .two}

::: {.panel}
**Lectures**

Build the conceptual and computational foundations.

You will mostly work through problems yourself so you understand **what the code is doing and why**.
:::

::: {.panel}
**Labs**

Apply those foundations to more extended problems.

Labs will be our primary setting for learning to work **productively and critically with AI**.
:::

::::

## AI in NTRES 6100

Generative AI is changing how people write code and conduct data analysis.

::: {.accent-box}
Our goal is **not** to learn how to have AI do the work for us.
:::

We will learn how to use AI while remaining responsible for:

- the scientific question
- analytical choices
- correctness of the code
- interpretation of the result
- reproducibility of the workflow

## A useful standard

::: {.hero}
“The code ran”  
**is not the same as**  
“the analysis is correct.”
:::

:::: {.card-row .two}

## Practice matters

::: {.hero}
Practice.  
Practice.  
**Practice.**
:::

::: {.aside}
Programming is learned by doing—not by watching someone else code.
:::

## Problem sets

- One problem set each week
- Applies class concepts in a new context
- Due the following **Thursday at 10 pm**
- Submitted through GitHub
- Each assignment will specify whether AI use is **restricted, permitted, or encouraged**

## To pass the course

You must:

- participate actively in class
- attend lectures unless other arrangements have been made
- submit at least **7 of 9** problem sets with demonstrated effort
- give a short end-of-course presentation showing how you are applying something from the course in your own work

## Now: R + RStudio

Today we will get oriented to:

- the RStudio IDE
- Console vs. Source
- objects and the Environment
- functions
- packages
- scripts
- projects
- help and autocomplete

## One important habit from Day 1

::: {.hero}
Work in an  
**RStudio Project**
:::

::: {.aside}
Avoid building workflows around `setwd()` and absolute file paths.
:::

## Another important habit

::: {.statement}
Do not save and restore `.RData` workspaces.
:::

A reproducible analysis should be recreated from **data + code + documented dependencies**—not from whatever happens to be sitting in your Environment.
